t.2.95.1: Having heard Rāma's words, Bharata replied: "What will the dharma of kings do for me, who am bereft of dharma?"
t.2.95.2: This eternal law has always held among us, O bull among men: while the eldest son stands, O king, a younger one may not become king.
t.2.95.3: Therefore, O Rāghava, go with me to prosperous Ayodhyā, and have yourself consecrated for the welfare of this family of ours.
t.2.95.4: They call a king a human being, but in my view he is held to be a god, the king whose conduct, joined with dharma and artha, they call superhuman.
t.2.95.5: While I was staying among the Kekayas and you had taken refuge in the forest, O noble one, the king, a devoted performer of sacrifices esteemed by the good, went to heaven.
t.2.95.6: Rise, O tiger among men, and let the water-offering be made for your father; I and this Śatrughna here have already made our offering of water.
t.2.95.8: Hearing those piteous words spoken by Bharata, which told of his father's death, Rāghava fell senseless.
t.2.95.7: For they say, O Rāghava, that whatever is offered by one who is dear becomes imperishable in the worlds of the ancestors, and you are indeed dear to your father.
t.2.95.9: Hearing the unpleasant thunderbolt of words spoken by Bharata, Rāma, scorcher of foes, flung up his arms and fell to the ground, like a tree with blossoming crown felled by an axe in the forest.
t.2.95.11: Those brothers, weeping together with Vaidehī, sprinkled with water the great archer, who was wasted all over by grief.
t.2.95.10: Thus Rāma, lord of the earth, lay fallen upon the earth, like an elephant asleep after wearing itself out battering a riverbank.
t.2.95.12: But Kākutstha, having regained consciousness, shedding tears from his eyes, began to speak piteously and at length.
t.2.95.13: What service, indeed, can be rendered by me, ill-born as I am, to that great-souled one, who died of grief for me and to whom I did not even give the funeral rites?
t.2.95.14: Ah, Bharata, the king has attained his purpose, since he was duly honored by you, O sinless one, and by Śatrughna in all the funeral rites.
t.2.95.15: Even when my dwelling in the forest has come to an end, I cannot bring myself to go to Ayodhyā, which is now without a leader, in disarray, and bereft of its lord of men.
t.2.95.16: O scorcher of foes, now that my father has gone to the other world, who will guide me again in Ayodhyā when my dwelling in the forest is completed?
t.2.95.17: Those words, so pleasing to the ear, which my father once spoke to me in affectionate comfort when he saw that I had conducted myself well, from where shall I now hear them?
t.2.95.18: Having spoken thus to Bharata, Rāghava, burning with grief, approached his wife, whose face was like the full moon, and spoke to her.
t.2.95.20: Having comforted the weeping daughter of Janaka, Rāma, himself grieved, then spoke sorrowful words there to Lakṣmaṇa.
t.2.95.19: Sītā, your father-in-law is dead; Lakṣmaṇa, you are bereft of your father. Bharata tells the sorrowful news that the lord of the earth has gone to heaven.
t.2.95.21: Bring the oil-cake of the iṅguda fruit, and fetch an upper garment of bark; I shall go to perform the water-offering for my great-souled father.
t.2.95.22: Let Sītā go in front; you walk close beside her; I shall follow behind, for this way is very dreadful.
t.2.95.23: Then came he who was ever their follower, a man who knew himself and was of great intelligence, gentle, self-controlled and tranquil, and possessed of firm devotion to Rāma.
t.2.95.24: Sumantra, together with those princes, comforted Rāghava and, supporting him, led him down into the auspicious river Mandākinī.
t.2.95.25: Then those illustrious ones, having with difficulty reached the lovely river Mandākinī, with its fine fords and its woods ever in bloom,
t.2.95.27: And the protector of the earth, taking up a cupped handful filled with water and facing the southern direction, the quarter of Yama, spoke these words while weeping.
t.2.95.26: Reaching the swift-flowing river at an auspicious ford free of mud, they poured out water for the king, saying, “Then let this be yours.”
t.2.95.28: O tiger among kings, may this pure, inexhaustible water offered by me reach you today, now that you have gone to the world of the ancestors.
t.2.95.29: Then, having come up out of the water onto the bank of the Mandākinī, that radiant Rāghava, together with his brothers, made the funeral offering to his father.
t.2.95.30: Having placed the iṅgudī oil-cake mixed with jujube fruits upon a spread of darbha grass, Rāma, sorely afflicted with grief and weeping, spoke these words.
t.2.95.32: Then, climbing back up from the riverbank by that very same path, the tiger among men ascended the mountain with its lovely slopes.
t.2.95.31: Eat this, great king, with pleasure, for this is what we ourselves eat; whatever food a man lives on, that same food is the food of his deities.
t.2.95.33: Then, having reached the door of the leaf-hut, the lord of the earth took hold of both Bharata and Lakṣmaṇa with his two hands.
t.2.95.34: From the sound of those brothers weeping together with Vaidehī, an echo arose on the mountain, as if from lions roaring.
t.2.95.35: Hearing that tumultuous sound, Bharata's soldiers were alarmed and said, "Surely Bharata has met with Rāma; this great clamour is theirs alone, as they grieve for their dead father."
t.2.95.36: Then all of them, abandoning their dwellings, turned toward that sound and, with a single mind, went running each from his own place.
t.2.95.37: Some men went on horses, others on elephants, others on well-adorned chariots, and likewise others, though delicately reared, went on foot.
t.2.95.38: Eager to see Rāma, who had been away only a short while yet seemed as if long absent, all the people went hastily to the hermitage.
t.2.95.39: But they, in haste and eager to see the meeting of the brothers, went forth in vehicles of many kinds, crowded with hooves and wheel-rims.
t.2.95.40: That earth, pounded by the hooves and wheel-rims of many vehicles, gave forth a tumultuous roar, like the sky when the clouds gather.
t.2.95.41: Terrified by that, the elephants, surrounded by their female elephants, then went away to another forest, perfuming it with their scent.
t.2.95.42: Boars, deer and lions, buffaloes together with bears and monkeys, tigers, gokarṇa antelopes and wild oxen fled in terror along with the spotted deer.
t.2.95.44: The sky was filled with birds frightened by that sound, and the earth was covered with men; both then shone forth splendidly.
t.2.95.43: The ruddy geese named after the chariot-wheel, the gallinules, swans, kāraṇḍava ducks and plava waterfowl, as well as the male cuckoos and the krauñca cranes, fled bewildered in every direction.
t.2.95.45: Then, seeing those men, their eyes filled with tears and deeply grieved, he who knew dharma embraced them as a father would and as a mother would.
t.2.95.47: Then the sound of those great-souled ones weeping, like the roll of mṛdaṅga drums, was heard unceasingly, echoing through the earth and the sky, the caves of the mountains, and the quarters of the world.
t.2.95.46: There he embraced some of the men, while others saluted him. Then the king's son, approaching all of them together with his friends and kinsmen, honoured each as he deserved.
